newsitem.title: BRAZIL: IMF chief blasts Brazil on trade - report.
newsitem.headline: IMF chief blasts Brazil on trade - report.

text.p: International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus hit out at Brazil's trade policy, including high-tariff barriers which protect the auto and textile industries, financial daily Gazeta Mercantil reported.
"In a world market like today's, no national industry can prosper with that kind of protection," Camdessus said in an interview published on Monday.
Camdessus urged Brazil to seek increased economic productivity by implementing real efficiencies and not through trade barriers or currency devaluation.

"In a situation of international competition, in all countries of the world -- including Brazil -- there is a temptation to obtain relief through currency devaluation or protectionism," the IMF chief told Gazeta. "However, every serious and responsible government, every independent central bank, must reject these measures, which are deadly for any economy," he said.

Camdessus was full of praise for Brazil's two year-old real anti-inflation plan which he said had re-introduced macroeconomic discipline to Brazil. "With the competitive advantages of a young country and so many human and natural resources, Brazil is already one of the world's major industrial powers," he said.
"(Brazil) has in its hands all the elements to continue in that direction, so long as it doesn't take any drugs that cause temporary euphoria and disregard effort."

Camdessus said the IMF was concerned about what it saw as Latin America's excessive reliance on foreign debt. He said the bank approved when proceeds were directed towards improving a country's productive capacity.
He cited Brazil as an example of a country with a manageable international debt level.
"When you compare your debt with the size of the Brazilian economy, its not that high: 21 percent of Gross Domestic Product.

"As Brazil moves forward in its stabilization and structural reform plan, it will be able to increasingly tap international capital markets. (Brazil) can do so. It has space to do so, so long as the resources are applied to strengthening the country's productive base. That is healthy, good and can help growth," said Camdessus.
